articles.summary: President Trump confirmed on Sunday he is considering moving the White House press corps from its historic location. “Also, I am not building a swimming pool in the White House Briefing Room, and never had any intention of doing so,” he wrote on Truth Social in a lengthy post about comedian Bill Maher. “I am…
articles.body:
President Trump confirmed on Sunday he is considering moving the White House press corps from its historic location.

“Also, I am not building a swimming pool in the White House Briefing Room, and never had any intention of doing so,” he wrote on Truth Social in a lengthy post about comedian Bill Maher. “I am thinking about moving the Press, and putting them in a different location, but I will use that location for very badly needed space.”

The confirmation comes after The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Trump expressed to aides he would like to bring back an indoor pool installed in 1933 during the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration. The pool was later covered under former President Richard Nixon to make space for the briefing room.

Trump has previously called the reports “Fake News” in a separate Truth Social post Saturday but hinted he “may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location.”

“The old swimming pool will never be brought back. I NEVER even thought to do such a stupid thing,” he continued.

The Trump administration has attempted multiple times to restrict press access to the White House and the Pentagon. Recently, The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg was removed from his print press pool duties by the White House after the president lashed out at the reporter in the Oval Office.

White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) President Jacqui Heinrich accused the White House of acting in “ retaliation ” and objected to the move.

Heinrich was also critical of the White House’s decision to bar Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House earlier this year. A federal judge issued a block on Trump’s ban of the three major news organizations, ruling that the outlets were likely not given enough due process.

Though CNN reporters, like Feinberg, are still unable to join the press pool on Air Force One.

A White House spokesperson told The Hill earlier this week, “no person and no journalist has a constitutional right to access the President’s Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities.”

“When publications lie, fabricate, and ignore the truth, proximity matters less and they can write their fiction from outside of these secure facilities,” the spokesperson continued.

articles.title: Nicki Minaj tells Trump she’ll support him if he runs again
articles.summary: Nicki Minaj joined President Trump at a campaign rally Sunday and said that she would support him if he chose to run again. “So, President Trump, it is an honor to stand with you every single time, and I will continue to support you forever and ever. If you run again, I will support you…
articles.body:
Nicki Minaj joined President Trump at a campaign rally Sunday and said that she would support him if he chose to run again.

“So, President Trump, it is an honor to stand with you every single time, and I will continue to support you forever and ever. If you run again, I will support you again,” Minaj said while campaigning with Trump in Michigan for former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

The singer who has dubbed herself as Trump’s “ No. 1 fan ” and has worked with the Trump administration on several initiatives — including the debut of the Trump Accounts — and traveled with administration officials aboard Air Force One to the rally.

White House communications director Steven Cheung even floated the possibility of her serving as the next Press Secretary. It’s unclear how serious Cheung is being about hiring Minaj as one of the administration’s top officials.

“Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House Press Secretary! @NICKIMINAJ,” he wrote on social platform X Sunday alongside a video of him and Minaj seated aboard Air Force One.

In the video, Minaj described Trump as “a man who’s won three elections.”

The comment references Trump falsely claiming that he won the 2020 election over former President Biden. The president stated in 2023 that the election was “rigged,” adding that there is video evidence of ballot boxes being stuffed.

Minaj continued, “[Trump] wakes up at 4o’clock in the morning. He outworks people that you know are half his age, and you know what does that say about his character? He knows that he will be fine.”

“He can kick his feet up and just, you know, chill out for the rest of his presidency. But no, he’s paying it forward,” the singer said. “He’s thinking about the other Republicans that have to win during these elections, and so that tells me that he’s a great guy.”

In 2020 Minaj said she would not “jump on the Donald Trump bandwagon,” but in recent years she’s become a vocal supporter of the president.

She has previously appeared at a Treasury Department-hosted summit in Washington to launch “Trump Accounts” for newborn babies and Turning Point USA’s annual conference.

articles.title: Trump dials up Islamophobia against Abdul El-Sayed at Michigan Senate rally
articles.summary: Al Jazeera looks at the key takeaways from the US president’s campaign event in Michigan ahead of the midterm vote.
articles.body:
Port Huron, Michigan – United States President Donald Trump has sharpened his anti-Muslim attacks against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, going so far as to suggest that Christmas would be cancelled if the progressive doctor won.

Trump visited Michigan on Sunday to shore up support for Republican candidates in the Midwestern state ahead of the midterm elections on November 3.

But from his podium, he levelled unfounded allegations against El-Sayed, including calling him a “jihadist”.

“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said of El-Sayed.

The president, whose popularity has been slipping in part due to the US-Israel war on Iran, spoke for nearly two hours to hundreds of supporters.

His remarks largely focused on Michigan’s Senate election, which is one of only about seven toss-up races for the upper chamber of Congress.

El-Sayed faces Republican candidate Mike Rogers for the state’s open Senate seat, and the race is considered crucial for Republicans to retain control of the 100-member Senate.

If Rogers wins, he would flip a seat currently held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, leaving Democrats with the difficult task of flipping five other seats to regain control of the chamber.

Currently, Republicans have a 53-seat majority in the Senate. Only 35 Senate positions are up for election in 2026.

Here are five key takeaways from the Republican event.

Trump doubles down on anti-Muslim attacks

While Trump has repeatedly targeted El-Sayed’s Muslim identity in recent weeks, including by misrepresenting the Democrat’s name as “Mohammed”, the US president took his rhetoric to new heights on Sunday.

Throughout the speech, Trump returned to themes related to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, falsely accusing the candidate of wanting to impose Islamic law in the US.

“So Abdul… also wants our country to go to Sharia law, and if he ever pulls that off, he should be the first one that’s tried. I’ll be a witness,” Trump said, apparently imagining El-Sayed being tried in a religious court.

Several times during the rally, some attendees blurted out “traitor” when El-Sayed’s name was mentioned.

“I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump said.

El-Sayed is a US-born citizen and former public health official who has pledged to uphold the Constitution. There is no evidence that he was ever a member of the Muslim Brotherhood or any foreign organisation.

Since Trump first ran for president during the 2016 election cycle, he has weaponised anti-Muslim bigotry for political gain.

In 2015, for instance – near the beginning of his first successful campaign – Trump said he would support “a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States”.

Less than two years later, Trump used the presidency to sign a short-lived executive order barring travel from multiple Muslim-majority countries, what became known as the “Muslim ban”.

In Sunday’s speech, Trump appealed once more to fears of Muslim immigration.

“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump said.

El-Sayed has previously largely dismissed the anti-Muslim rhetoric against him as an attempt to create “distractions”, saying he is focused more on domestic issues, including lowering the cost of living and expanding access to healthcare.

With Trump’s approval ratings plummeting, some Republican candidates in tight races have kept their distance from the president.

Rogers has previously called for an end to the Iran war and expressed reservations about Trump’s tariff campaign, urging an end to the trade war with Canada, which borders Michigan.

But Rogers attended Sunday’s rally and took the stage alongside Trump in a display of mutual support.

A survey by the research firm Marketing Resource Group suggested earlier this month that only 35 percent of voters in Michigan view Trump positively.

Rogers set the tone for the anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed earlier in the rally, also claiming the Democrat is connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, a political movement in Egypt designated as a “terrorist” group by the US this year.

As a congressman, however, Rogers voted in 2012 to continue US aid to Egypt under Muslim Brotherhood President Mohamed Morsi.

In Sunday’s speech, Rogers also tried to paint El-Sayed as part of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), but unlike other progressives, El-Sayed is not a member of the left-wing group.

“This DSA-affiliated candidate is also taking a lot of money from organizations that support the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah,” Rogers said, without offering evidence.

All three groups are designated as “terrorist” organisations in the US, making it illegal to provide any material support to them.

On Sunday, the average price of a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol in Michigan was $4.83, up from $2.91 before the start of the war on Iran.

Tehran has restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz in response to the war, sending energy prices soaring.

Trump initially promised the conflict would only last four to six weeks.

But nearly eight months after the US and Israel launched the war on February 28, the conflict is showing no signs of concluding.

On Sunday, Trump said he has no regrets about the war.

“I made that decision, and I have no second guess,” Trump told the crowd.

He added that he thought petrol prices would have increased by much more than they had. He also defended his decision by referencing the threat of nuclear warfare.

“The number one state sponsor of terror is Iran by far, and we had to make sure they didn’t have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.

Iran has denied seeking a nuclear weapon. It has long argued its uranium enrichment programme is for civilian energy production.

Before the war, Trump also argued that US strikes against Iran’s uranium enrichment facilities in June 2025 had completely “obliterated” the country’s nuclear programme.

Despite the economic anxiety related to the cost of living and skyrocketing petrol prices, Trump bragged about the amount of profit US oil companies are making from the war.

Demand for energy products has increased globally in recent months, as supply chains tighten.

“Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East, because they’re coming to Texas, and they’re coming to Oklahoma, and they’re coming to Louisiana, and they’re taking that oil,” Trump said. “They’re making hundreds of billions of dollars.”

Trump added that his advisers asked him not to bring up this issue because “people are paying a little higher” for petrol and gas.

“I could just see the fake headline: ‘President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump.’ That’ll be the headline. I said, ‘I don’t give a damn. I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune,'” the US president said.

Trump can still mobilise Republican base

A line of Trump supporters stretched several blocks outside the rally on Sunday.

Attendees, dressed in Make America Great Again (MAGA) gear, filled the hockey arena where Trump spoke.

The crowd roared and laughed with Trump, with attendees frequently blurting out expressions of admiration for the president and insults against his opponents, especially El-Sayed.

Trump may appear politically on the back foot amid dwindling popularity and mounting anger over inflation and the Iran war.

But the president has highlighted his continued ability to mobilise his core MAGA base, often pointing to his crowd size as a metric for his success as a campaigner.

The audience remained engaged and seated throughout the speech on Sunday.

At one point, the address took a bizarre turn as the president spoke about the backside of Jon Husted, a Republican incumbent from Ohio competing in another tight Senate race.

“I looked at his a**, and I’ve never done that with a man before. Women? Yes. Men? No,” Trump said.

The US president also complimented the derriere of the rapper Nicki Minaj, one of his prominent supporters in attendance.

“By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful a** before: Nicki Minaj. That’s hard to miss,” Trump said.

articles.title: Midterms unleash what may be the nastiest barrage of attack ads yet
articles.summary: From Vivek Ramaswamy's toxic Ohio ad to Ken Paxton's AI-generated spots in Texas, the 2026 midterms are now drowning in political attack ads.
articles.body: It’s last-minute garbage time as the midterms are just over a week away, with candidates uncorking their dirtiest ads, their filthiest charges and their ugliest rhetoric. This barrage is fueled as never before by social media, and a surging public interest since any one of a dozen states could tip the battle for Senate control. I feel like taking a shower. The chairman of Montana’s Democratic Party, Shannon O’Brien, just resigned, underscoring the extreme sensitivity to national politics. The party, she said in an MS NOW essay, "is more divided than ever not because of our values but because of the race for the U.S. Senate… The winner of this race will almost certainly vote on a nominee to the Supreme Court." THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND O’Brien said there are "real questions" about the Democratic candidate’s views on such issues as abortion and poverty. Virginia’s Democratic state senator L. Louise Lucas was just indicted on federal charges including racketeering conspiracy and money laundering conspiracy, related to her co-ownership of a cannabis business. The probe predates the Trump administration, but Lucas vowed to fight back: "I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them." It’s like an echo chamber. President Trump has already nationalized the election by saying people should vote as if he’s on the ballot–and barnstorming with increasingly tough talk about the Democrats. A local council member in suburban Des Moines, Shellie Flockhart, appeared in an ad ripping a Democratic candidate as "just plain dangerous" for kids–but the Washington Post reported that she once pleaded guilty to child endangerment after driving drunk with two of her children. A splashy piece in Vanity Fair, containing allegations against Jared Kushner, just happened to come out now, prompting Kushner’s lawyer to put the magazine on notice of a potential lawsuit. The attorney for the president’s son-in-law argued that Vanity Fair had failed after repeated requests to produce "a single bank statement, wire transfer record, account number, or other verifiable evidence supporting these extraordinary accusations." DNC LAWSUIT ACCUSES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OF DIVERTING $20M IN FEDERAL FUNDS FOR 'PROPAGANDA' ADS The article, which Kushner calls "completely insane," is based on a forthcoming book claiming that Russian security services hacked his phone, disclosing $700 million in secret foreign transactions, and that his signature is on an account set up by Saudi Arabia and the UAE. The timing sounds more than coincidental. Embed: After decades of political coverage, I immediately knew that the toxic ad by Vivek Ramaswamy–featuring Democrat Amy Acton’s long-estranged mother calling her a liar–would be more than just an issue in the Ohio governor’s race. I sensed that it would quickly become a national referendum on sleaziness. The mother, Donna Arthur, sided with her second husband, even though Cledith Arthur was indicted for raping Amy Acton when she was 12 years old. The couple disappeared, and the stepfather was never tried before his death. Acton has had no contact with her mother since 1978. To their credit, many Republicans, led by Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, have denounced the ad. Trump has defended it as fair game, saying he doesn’t know anything about a stepfather and that Democrats would certainly use such an ad against him. In far lesser-known races, the mudslinging grows by the day. In Texas, Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz is sending a torrent of emails about her opponent, saying "Bobby Pulido is unfit to serve in Congress." When his fellow bandmate "was arrested on a child rape charge, Bobby went to his uncle, the crooked district attorney, and the charge disappeared along with three other felonies. Gone." ‘CAN’T TRUST AMY ACTON’: VIRAL AD DISTRACTS FROM WHAT’S REALLY AT STAKE IN CRITICAL RACE, GOP STRATEGIST SAYS Pulido told Politico that he never knew about his onetime accordionist’s child molestation charges more than a decade ago. "I’ve apologized for everything that I’ve ever joked about that offended anybody… There’s a lot of tweets in there that I’m embarrassed of. There’s jokes that I’ve told that I apologize for," he said. But the Washington Free Beacon says Pulido "has given shifting stories and conflicting information surrounding his child molester bandmate." In the more prominent Senate race in Texas between Ken Paxton and James Talarico, the attorney general has been running an AI-generated spot saying his Democratic opponent "voted for an income tax" and "Texans can’t afford Talarico’s radical agenda." Fact-checkers call the income tax charge false, and Talarico’s response ad says, "I don’t have to use AI, because the truth about Ken Paxton is bad enough." But how many voters, in Texas and across the country, will take the time to sort out such charges and counter-charges? How many will just tune out the high-decibel attacks? How many will hit the mute button? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Personally, I feel numb after scrutinizing the seemingly endless barrage on the airwaves. I fact-checked ads for five presidential cycles, but this is dirtier and more unhinged than ever. And the crucial question for 2026: How many voters will just stay home?

articles.title: Lula da Silva se impone a Flávio Bolsonaro y es reelecto presidente de Brasil
articles.standfirst: El presidente remonta la primera vuelta y logra un cuarto mandato; su rival pedirá anular los comicios
articles.summary: El presidente remonta la primera vuelta y logra un cuarto mandato; su rival pedirá anular los comicios
articles.body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva fue reelegido este domingo, 25 de octubre, como presidente de Brasil tras vencer en la segunda vuelta al senador ultraderechista Flávio Bolsonaro. El líder del Partido de los Trabajadores obtuvo el 51,79% de los votos válidos, frente al 48,21% de su rival, una diferencia cercana a los 4,4 millones de sufragios, según el Tribunal Superior Electoral. Con este triunfo, Lula, de 80 años, se convierte en el primer presidente brasileño que accede a un cuarto mandato, el segundo consecutivo, que arrancará en enero de 2027. El resultado supone un vuelco respecto a la primera vuelta, en la que el hijo mayor de Jair Bolsonaro se impuso con un 47% de los votos frente al 45% del mandatario. Las últimas encuestas de Datafolha y Quaest situaban a ambos en empate técnico e, incluso, otorgaban una ligera ventaja al senador. El escrutinio fue de infarto: Lula abrió con ventaja, Bolsonaro lo superó cuando se había contado en torno al 14% de los votos y el presidente recuperó el primer puesto en la recta final. Lula agradeció la participación de los jóvenes y aseguró que gobernará para todos los brasileños. Flávio Bolsonaro, candidato del Partido Liberal, anunció que no reconocerá los resultados y que su equipo jurídico pedirá la anulación de los comicios. El senador cuestiona la decisión del juez del Supremo Tribunal Federal Cristiano Zanin, al que describió como exabogado de Lula, de prolongar dos horas la votación en todo el país por problemas de transporte público. Según Bolsonaro, la medida se adoptó a las 17.01, justo cuando debían cerrar los colegios, y cambió las reglas en plena partida. La prórroga se ordenó principalmente a petición de la campaña de Lula, aunque la del propio Bolsonaro había solicitado antes una ampliación limitada a cinco estados. El presidente del Tribunal Superior Electoral, Kassio Nunes Marques, admitió que la medida cautelar dictada tras el cierre oficial generó dificultades en el proceso, aunque la justicia electoral garantizó el recuento.
